expectedText:
BEREAVEMENT LEAVE — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

BEREAVEMENT LEAVE REQUEST
Jordan Lee requests bereavement leave from Acme, Inc. as described below.

Family member (relationship): _______________________________________________
Date of death: _______________
Dates of leave requested (need not be consecutive): _______________________________________________
Total days requested (up to 5): _______________
Documentation of death, if requested by Acme, Inc. within 30 days of the first day of leave, will be provided separately.

BEREAVEMENT LEAVE ENTITLEMENT
Under California law, it is an unlawful employment practice for a covered employer to refuse a covered employee's request to take up to five days of bereavement leave upon the death of a family member. The five days need not be taken consecutively. For this purpose, "family member" means a spouse, child, parent, sibling, grandparent, grandchild, domestic partner, or parent-in-law.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "It shall be an unlawful employment practice for an employer to refuse to grant a request by any employee to take up to five days of bereavement leave upon the death of a family member."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.7 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.7(b)-(c), bereavement leave entitlement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12945.7)
  "“Family member” means a spouse or a child, parent, sibling, grandparent, grandchild, domestic partner, or parent-in-law as defined in Section 12945.2."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.7 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.7(a)(3), definition of “family member” (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12945.7)
  Known gap: Five days is a ceiling this statute sets, not a floor every workplace defaults to in the same way — how those days interact with an employer's own bereavement policy is a separate question addressed elsewhere in this document. The statute's family-member list is mostly self-defining, but "parent-in-law" is defined by cross-reference to the California Family Rights Act (Gov. Code § 12945.2); that cross-referenced CFRA definition was not independently fetched or verified for this document, so it isn't restated here. This document also doesn't cover a separate carve-out in the statute for employees covered by certain collective bargaining agreements that already provide equivalent bereavement leave.

EMPLOYER COVERAGE
This bereavement leave requirement applies to an "employer," defined as a person who employs five or more persons to perform services for a wage or salary, as well as to the state and any of its political or civil subdivisions, including cities and counties.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "“Employer” means either of the following: (A) A person who employs five or more persons to perform services for a wage or salary. (B) The state and any political or civil subdivision of the state, including, but not limited to, cities and counties."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.7 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.7(a)(2), definition of “employer” (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12945.7)
  Known gap: The five-employee threshold tracks the general coverage threshold used elsewhere in California's Fair Employment and Housing Act, of which this section is part, but this document doesn't verify that every other FEHA provision uses an identical threshold — only that this specific bereavement leave provision does.

EMPLOYEE ELIGIBILITY
For purposes of this leave, an "employee" is a person who has been employed by the employer for at least 30 days before the leave begins. The statute separately excludes from this definition a person covered by Government Code section 19859.3.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "“Employee” means a person employed by the employer for at least 30 days prior to the commencement of the leave."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.7 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.7(a)(1)(A), definition of “employee” (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12945.7)
  "“Employee” does not include a person who is covered by Section 19859.3."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.7 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.7(a)(1)(B), exclusion from “employee” definition (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12945.7)
  Known gap: This document verified and quotes the 30-day threshold and the fact of the section 19859.3 exclusion directly from the statute, but did not separately fetch or verify the text of section 19859.3 itself, so it doesn't describe what that excluded category covers.

TIMING AND PAID/UNPAID STATUS
The bereavement leave must be completed within three months of the family member's date of death. The leave is taken under the employer's own existing bereavement leave policy, if it has one. If the employer has no existing bereavement leave policy, the leave may be unpaid, except that the employee may use vacation, personal leave, accrued and available sick leave, or compensatory time off that is otherwise available.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The bereavement leave shall be completed within three months of the date of death of the family member."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.7 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.7(d), timing of leave (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12945.7)
  "The bereavement leave shall be taken pursuant to any existing bereavement leave policy of the employer."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.7 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.7(e)(1)-(2), paid/unpaid status (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12945.7)
  "If there is no existing bereavement leave policy, the bereavement leave may be unpaid, except that an employee may use vacation, personal leave, accrued and available sick leave, or compensatory time off that is otherwise available to the employee."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.7 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.7(e)(2), default unpaid status absent an employer policy (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12945.7)
  Known gap: This is a floor, not a formula for every scenario: the statute separately addresses what happens when an employer's existing policy provides fewer than five days of paid leave, or fewer than five days of unpaid leave, topping each up to a five-day minimum in different ways — those blending rules aren't restated in this clause. The statute doesn't create a freestanding state-paid bereavement benefit; payment, where it exists, comes from the employer's own policy or the employee's own accrued paid leave.

DOCUMENTATION OF DEATH
If the employer requests it within 30 days of the first day of leave, the employee must provide documentation of the family member's death. "Documentation" includes, but isn't limited to, a death certificate, a published obituary, or written verification of death, burial, or memorial services from a mortuary, funeral home, burial society, crematorium, religious institution, or governmental agency. The employer must maintain the confidentiality of any employee requesting this leave, and any documentation the employee provides must be kept confidential and disclosed only to internal personnel or counsel as necessary, or as otherwise required by law.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The employee, if requested by the employer, within 30 days of the first day of the leave, shall provide documentation of the death of the family member. As used in this subdivision, “documentation” includes, but is not limited to, a death certificate, a published obituary, or written verification of death, burial, or memorial services from a mortuary, funeral home, burial society, crematorium, religious institution, or governmental agency."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.7 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.7(f), documentation the employer may require (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12945.7)
  "The employer shall maintain the confidentiality of any employee requesting leave under this section. Any documentation provided to the employer pursuant to subdivision (f) or subdivision (g) shall be maintained as confidential and shall not be disclosed except to internal personnel or counsel, as necessary, or as required by law."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.7 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.7(i), confidentiality of leave request and documentation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12945.7)
  Known gap: The statute gives examples of acceptable documentation rather than a fixed, exclusive list ("includes, but is not limited to"), so what satisfies a given employer's request beyond those examples is not fixed by this text alone.

NO RETALIATION OR DISCRIMINATION
This same statute makes it a separate unlawful employment practice for an employer to refuse to hire, or to discharge, demote, fine, suspend, expel, or discriminate against, an individual because that individual exercised the right to bereavement leave, or gave information or testimony about their own or someone else's bereavement leave in a related inquiry or proceeding. It is likewise unlawful for an employer to interfere with, restrain, or deny the exercise of, or the attempt to exercise, any right this section provides.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "It shall be an unlawful employment practice for an employer to refuse to hire, or to discharge, demote, fine, suspend, expel, or discriminate against, an individual because of either of the following: (1) An individual’s exercise of the right to bereavement leave provided by subdivision (b). (2) An individual’s giving information or testimony as to their own bereavement leave, or another person’s bereavement leave, in an inquiry or proceeding related to rights guaranteed under this section."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.7 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.7(g), retaliation for exercising or discussing bereavement leave rights (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12945.7)
  "It shall be an unlawful employment practice for an employer to interfere with, restrain, or deny the exercise of, or the attempt to exercise, any right provided under this section."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.7 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.7(h), interference with the right to bereavement leave (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12945.7)
  Known gap: This anti-retaliation protection is written directly into this bereavement leave statute itself (Gov. Code § 12945.7(g)-(h)) — it is not solely a byproduct of FEHA's general anti-retaliation provisions elsewhere in the code, though it operates as an unlawful employment practice within that same statutory scheme.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT
Please sign below to acknowledge this bereavement leave request and the terms above.

Employee: Jordan Lee
Date: _______________

—
